utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Dr. Barr. Good morning, Madam Registrar, if you could be kind enough to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All the accused are here. I'm looking at the Defence Bench. I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes and of Mr. Meek. I think that's all. From the Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Soljan. Anybody else? No. Dr. Barr, good morning, once more. We are supposed to conclude with your testimony pretty soon, I suppose. There were only two Defence teams that put questions to you yesterday. So I'm going to ask Mr. Ostojic first whether he has furthers questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Barr?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did notice that you had some examination notes and also what you considered to be a tick sheets I think you called them?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Those are actually quite frankly very limited, are they not? For example, on the first Jokic report you have two and a half to three pages of examination notes, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's in there. And then you have a one page document which I think is classified as a tick sheet, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I didn't notice in the binder that was produced last night was any evidence in your file of the peer review or quality assurance by these "independent" document examiners that you mentioned. Were you able to find that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they've signed my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did not see that. Where is that? I'm looking over it and I see it. Would you be, with the Court's the permission, be kind enough to place that on the ELMO just so that we can see it or have the usher assist us in that regard? That would be a draft report or your final report.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My final report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who signed it, both of them?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made a mistake yesterday when I said that it was Dr. Hardcastle, Dr. Baxendale, it was actually Dr. Hardcastle who did it which is the top signature. The bottom signature is the person who proof read.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you have the same signatures for the other reports, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, with respect to your tick sheet, if I could direct your attention to the May 27, 2006 report, and if we could also place that on the ELMO just so we could all understand what a tick sheet is.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is it for, which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For Trbic.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Trbic or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's dated on top. It's not numbered in any manner but it's dated the 27th of May, 06, at the top right-hand corner. It's captioned as official duty officer logbook.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could show it to me I could find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure. In any event, I think we can still proceed unless you think you might need it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'll see. I mean I can use -- if you want that back.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I could read it -- if you leave it on the ELMO, I think we can both share it. Would that be okay to share it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Now is this what you call a tick sheet where you highlight each letter character on a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Other than the printed material that you have there, the other material is your handwritten notes, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What does it signify after the letter "A" and then "a," what is the note after that? What does it indicate?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates a match.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So every time you write this down, you would only record the matches but not the differences?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would record differences if I found them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How would you denote the differences?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally with a cross or a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the symbol I see that you have on some of these the symbols a dash -- or I'll strike that, a check mark. Do you see that? Or what I consider to be a check mark. I think I even highlighted it for you, did I not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what's the significance or how would I interpret that check mark on your tick sheet?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a match between the writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you use other symbols from time to time?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how about a dash or a negative or a minus sign?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minus sign normally means that I can't compare it because the characters aren't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can know that are there any other symbols that you might use when you do your tick sheet and assessment of the various letter characters for handwriting examination?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn actually now to the one that interests me most; although, I use it kind of as guide and that's the one relating to Mr. Jokic. Can you find that tick sheet for me and place it on the ELMO, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the one dated the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think so. I'm trying to catch up with you. The one that actually has the question marks and the dash marks and the other symbols we've just discussed. Yeah, the 11th of July is perfect, in fact. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in this one I see that the A has a question mark. Does it not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that means that it was not a match, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it means it wasn't a good match.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Based on your definition you just gave us moments ago, a question mark would indicate not a match as opposed to what you're suggesting now that it was not a good match?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said crosses were not a match.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look into that. What about the B you have two symbols there, one the abbreviation okay and a question mark. What does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means it's not as good as an okay, but it's better than a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the letter E what does that indicate? I mean the dash or the negative sign.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means there weren't any Es to compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay but let me ask you this. You took from Mr. Jokic his sample which he copied the exact question specimen of all ten pages. Didn't he just rewrite verbatim as we discussed yesterday each of these things?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did but this is the tick sheet for my original examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't have that at the time?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't get the sample handwriting until January.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Explain to me after your first report the second report you say that you were unable to give a definite opinion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in your third report, you also highlight that you were unable to give a definite opinion with respect to the question of whether or not this was Mr. Jokic's handwriting, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Why, if you had more material, did you not state in your first opinion or in your first report that you were unable to give a definite opinion in connection with Mr. Jokic's handwriting versus the questioned handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did in my first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Show it to me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: Counsel and witness are kindly asked to observe pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank the interpreters for that and I hope -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What paragraph is it, please?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it's a difference in terminology. I state that there is stronger, not conclusive evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But in each of your subsequent reports when you had more data meaning more sample specimens of Mr. Jokic, you conclude even though the Prosecutor asked to you give him a more definitive, if you will, opinion on Mr. Jokic, you concluded on the subsequent reports that you cannot give a definite opinion, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my last report that the middle report was just clarifying the first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But in both the middle report and the last report that's what you state, is it not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is what I stated in the first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That you do not have a definite opinion?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you this, if I may, I saw in the notes or materials that we reviewed or I reviewed yesterday a little synopsis about your company. It says that there are seven people working there, at least at that time, who are document examiners. Can you confirm with me that there are seven or are there more now?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nine working as well -- eight working as document examiners, one is a trainee.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who is Mike Allen?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is one of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is he also a document examiner?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Still with the company?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, were you ever asked to determine how many individuals wrote entries in the pages numbered 02935743 through 02935753, which are the ten pages we've been discussing briefly here yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me direct your attention to your own file and a letter from Peter boils dated the 27th of June 2003.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You have it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the page he states or asks you a question after he gives you some identification with the same numbers, right, 02935743 to 029352 -- 5753, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you see in the middle he asks, "How many individuals wrote entries in pages [numbered]" -- and then just to shorten it ending in 5743 through 5753]. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So in fact they did ask you, meaning the Prosecution, to tell them how many individuals wrote the entries in those pages, did they not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, this actually is not stating exactly what is on this letter. If we could place it on the ELMO perhaps to see how that was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that because we don't have it available right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we might have to scroll down a little because it's in the middle of the page starting with the first dash mark where it says "how many"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: It says is it -- the only thing that is asked there is is it possible to ascertain the following and then there is also a note in handwriting. I just wanted to indicate that for the record. So saying this is not actually to commence work but simply saying general question of is it possible to ascertain this kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now you've made your point. I think we can proceed. The Dr. Barr has the document in front of her. I think she's familiar with it more than anyone else in this courtroom. There is in no point in discussing it further. Please proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I've not discussed it at all, Mr. President just waiting to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to discuss it just proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Barr is this the first correspondence that you received from the Office of the Prosecution requesting that you work on this project?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what was it, the second, third, maybe fourth because you're report is actually the first one is generated, what, the 17th or 16th of July of 2003, right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this correspondence we see is the 27th of June, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, whether or not as my learned colleague thinks the question was perhaps not as clearly of you, my question to you I thought was quite clear: Did anyone ask you to determine if it was possible how many individuals wrote the entries in those ten pages, did they?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did -- who else can we go to to answer this question if not a forensic document examiner? Would you think of any other specialty in this field?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Really the only person in order to be able to give us that answer would indeed be a forensic handwriting expert, would it not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you come up with an answer for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that wasn't what they ultimately asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have the ultimate letter for that which they asked. Do you have it? Because I know your correspondence was divided from the left side of the binder and the right side and we agreed that we were only going to take that which was contained on the right side of your file, but I did specifically ask for that correspondence. In any event, not to waste too much of your time we will get it hopefully at the end of the day today. Now, you list out in during your biography and when you provided us a copy or a synopsis of your company's work four specific tools that are utilised in forensic handwriting analysis, and we talked about some of them yesterday, the EDSA and then the video microscope and I think you also mention in your profile that there is a binocular stereo microscopes?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then the final tool which I wasn't familiar with was something called a docucentre 3.000?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you were talking about before with the ultraviolet and infrared lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's just the name of the manufacturer?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Out of the four tools that your company says that it provides and has available to them in order to complete forensic document examination, can you tell us out of those four which did you utilise in your examination in the five reports that you generated?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the binocular microscope.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I don't -- okay. You can now because it has come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Barr, what I'd like to ask you is to direct your attention to your examination notes, please, for Mr. Jokic that were taken in July of 03. And if you could just summarise for me your technique that you use, as I mention at the beginning you have approximately two and a half to three pages of these notes broken down into two parts. One I think what you do is basically look at the material that was provided for you and make an index of each page with some notations on it; and then secondly what do you is go through what we call the assessment which is in the last half page which is the handwriting comparison, I think you call it, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you that for each and every report?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the amount of writing there was. It may not be in exactly the same style, but same basic principles would be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now Comparing that to your tick sheet where on some you have certain symbols on it, when there is no symbol, what does that denote?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some of those that's just a specimen writing, so I only put the symbols on the writing that I'm actually comparing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the tick sheet that you had?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And whether you write actually next to the letter A, you write two or more letters in your own handwriting, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sometimes you put a question mark?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel and witness are kindly asked to make pauses between question and answer. It is impossible to translate at this rate of speed without pauses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Ostojic and Dr. Barr. Please do understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I most definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have difficulties and sometimes we can have in the background also the interpretation both in French and in B/C/S so it's a problem for them. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'd like to just ask you very straightforward and when you have your tick sheet you have the letter that's printed out already on this tick sheet, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then next to any given letter, let's take A for example since it's the first letter, when you write in other letters what does that denote?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's when I'm going through and looking at the different character constructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So if you have two letters you have found two different character constructions of that letter A?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if you have more than that it's whatever number you've found, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an aide-memoire, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what does the fact that there is no symbol indicated in the box which corresponds to the letter character, what does that denote, if anything?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on which specific tick sheet you were looking at, clearly when I do the specimen writing, I don't make a annotation on it because that's my initial examination of the specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you only do it for the questioned writing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your first report for Mr. Jokic did you have a specimen writing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I couldn't find the tick sheet for that specimen writing but was only able to find the questioned writing. If I understood your notes properly and that is because you have a Q with a exponential indication above it indicating that that's the questioned specimen, would I be right on that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if there was no letter written on your tick sheet which has the questioned specimen meaning no writings by you, does that indicate that you were unable to find that letter, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when there is no symbol attached to that section, what does that indicate again meaning question mark, dash mark, hash mark or?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally it would mean that it was the specimen writing that I was looking at. The specimen writing for Mr. Jokic is -- it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I only have the two pages of your tick sheet from Mr. Jokic which has the Q on it which goes through the alphabet and then the next page is just a new numeric 0 through 9, I believe?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does the peer review or the two people that looked at your work, did they actually go through the specimen writing and the questioned writing or did they merely just go through your notes meaning your tick sheet and your examination notes in order to verify whether or not your opinion is reasonable?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would go through the specimen and questioned writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would they also creates examination notes and tick sheets?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How would they then do the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, again you're doing exactly the same thing as before. I mean, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Barr is complying more or less but you aren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was concentrating on that more than the other and I'll focus more on concentrating on both. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But please allow a short pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can assist you, take out the headphones, set the channel to the 5 or 6, French or B/C/S and turn up the volume, when it's finished start to answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Should I keep the head phone on my shoulders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to you but you always forget to put a pause. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We were discussing briefly how the peer review or quality assurance aspect works, and if they wouldn't keep their notes or create examination notes or tick sheets in particular, how would they be able to verify or later how can anyone verify that in fact they did what they were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you have to take that on trust I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is your report that was filed in the case of Jokic, the three reports, did each of them have the signature by this peer review examiner who agreed with your opinions?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't find them but some of the photocopying was rather faint, so that's why I'm asking you. Would you mind just double checking for me?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I may show you or you have it here, you were also given an Annex B from the Office of the Prosecution to some correspondence which seemed to indicate that you were going to review all of the questioned handwriting from what we called the notebook, 377, which is the green book in front of you. Now, did you at any time, were you able to review the entire book in its -- completely?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With regard to the area that they were retaining you to do, and that is to check the handwriting analysis as it may relate to four separate individuals.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check what they asked me to do precisely in the first -- the second one. My understanding of this one was that they asked me originally for the four pages, the ten pages, and latterly for specific dates within the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what about the subsequent one?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subsequent one was for specific dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at Annex B and under paragraph 2, it identifies it as the unofficial duty officer notebook with the ERN number starting with 0293-5619 through 0293-5806. And then under A it reads, "July 12th through 17th inclusive dates" and it gives you the ERN number again, 0293-5730 through 5777. Compare handwriting on those dates, pages, to known handwriting.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you show me what you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission if the usher can show her her document that we received yesterday? First because it's highlighted, to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've ever seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was in your folder that I received in this binder yesterday afternoon. And I'm confident that my learned friend the Prosecution who is reading it herself that that's the case, I would think. In fact you had a couple different annexes all identified as Annex B. I can show you those too. Maybe they can help you find it. If I may, Your Honour. I'm handing two separate ones, one Annex B and then the other one I think says handwriting questions. Okay. If you didn't have it, we can clarify that later, if you say you never saw that and it's not part of your file, I'm sure the Prosecution will provide us with an explanation on that. I assume since they produced it to me yesterday that it's something that was in your file because that's what I asked for, your file. My next question is when you write --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just say you gave me three sheets. I've seen one of them not the other two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I was focuses on the first one I gave you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to assist you by giving you others that the Prosecution offered to me. Which one did you see of the three?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that's not labelled Annex B.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And Annex B of either one or two you've never seen before?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the two -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They are slightly different.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are slightly different, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to -- we'll clear that up, thank you for your candour on that. If I can have those back? That would be grateful -- I would be grateful. So it's fair to say that you -- even though you did have all the pages of the logbook, you did not go back to determine which if any were from these known handwritings of any known individual such as Jokic, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you did the Trbic, Nikolic and Strbac material, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One last question on the tick sheet, on some of them when you look at the 28th of June, 2006, you have actually written notes on the box of the tick sheet as opposed to just symbols. Do you know why you differentiate and sometimes have a written note versus a symbol and what if any is the significance between the two if any?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just a way of -- for me to remember what exactly it is that I considered was significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that which, even though yesterday we talked briefly about differences and similarities, there is nothing in your tick sheet which we can at least quantify to show how many symbols you considered to be similar and how many were considered different in any given time, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because there is no way in a handwriting examination of denoting -- you can't say that, for example, 15 similarities would make it a good match. It's the significance of those and it's difficult -- I tend to try and write those down, which I think I have in my notes, but the tick sheet is there as a way I'm actually comparing the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would that also be true if you utilised more than one of the tools available to you at your place of employment?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could -- the video microscope is simply a means of producing printouts of the handwriting. So it isn't really relevant. The docucentre is the means of determining the number of inks. Again it's not really relevant to a handwriting comparison. And the ESDA is a way of looking at indented impressions so again, it would not be relevant to a handwriting comparison. So for a handwriting comparison what I used would be what I would use in all handwriting comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the only thing you would use, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I noticed this in those ten pages you that reviewed with respect to Mr. Jokic on the photocopies that you have in your binder you had written little notations to yourself on it. For example, you'd write an arrow and then say something to the effect of blue ink. And then you'd write an arrow underneath that and say this was in black ink. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you do that on all material that you usually receive or --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what the case is. In this case I want to distinguish the fact that there were different inks on different pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did do you that on each and every page?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why on some and not on others?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I think it was because it started off it was a different writer in the black ink, so I was trying to distinguish between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Barr. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, do you have further questions for Dr. Barr.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, no further questions for Dr. Barr, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, you'll be pleased to hear that there are no further questions for you and that you are -- yes, Ms. Soljan has --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting, Your Honours, but I believe Mr. Bourgon ended up assigning a little bit of homework for Dr. Barr yesterday, and so we provided her with the original notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he has no further questions for her.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to note that for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If she has done the -- indeed, that question, and if she has an answer I would be glad to hear what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I go back on what I stated earlier: You've heard the exchange if you can enlighten us on your findings please go ahead, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously the circumstances in which I did it are less than ideal, but I would say that there is at least some limited evidence that the two pages on the one side were written by the same person who wrote the most -- that entry on the right-hand side of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you again, Doctor, and just to confirm what we are talking about in terms of the pages.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon for that. I was precisely going to ask Dr. Barr to refer us to the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So this refers to your report dated -- that's your report dated 29 June 2006, and this specific question related to paragraph 6.11, and what you are telling us now is that at page 02935760, there are two lines that according to you do not belong to Mr. Nikolic and there is writing at the top of page 02935761 which also don't belong to Mr. Nikolic but the same person would have written those two parts, to the best of your ability at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, doctor. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I can confirm that there are no further questions for you and that you're free to go. On behalf of the Tribunal and my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost and Judge Stole, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony and we all wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may Your Honour before we get to the exhibits I would like to know what Annex B is and how we received it yesterday, both those copies, and I tried to invite the Prosecutor to say that even though Dr. Barr was still here. I'd like to get clarification on it how that came to us and just so that the record is clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, after my learned friend's inquiry yesterday to get the notes, we immediately had them copied. As you may have seen, there are ample notes among those. We made sure that we photocopied everything that was on the right-hand sides as well as to include any writing that was there. What is in the binder that Mr. Ostojic was provided in was what was in her notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Only if I can clarify just to make sure I didn't find this and put it in the binder, that was given to us yesterday by the Prosecutor. I just want to make that clear, whether Dr. Barr remembers that or not is a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, documents to tender? Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would like to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I need to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: We would like to tender the report dated January 2007 which is P02844. Dr. Barr's report dated 29 June 2006 which is P02845. The report dated 16 July 2003 which is P02846, the report dated 22 August, 2003, which is P02847, the report dated 27 January 2004, which is P02848, Dr. Kathryn Barr's curriculum vitae dated 20 November 2006 which is P02849, the 65 ter number 935 which is the IKM log, the 65 ter number 345, which is the Zvornik Brigade report Bijeljina military Prosecutor dated 26 July 1995, and the selection of specimen and questioned document samples which is P02850, as well as PIC 00133 which is the selection of specimen and questioned documents which was marked by the witness on 25 June 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soljan. Any objections from the Defence teams? Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just trying to digest it, Your Honour. We do have an objection to the last two, I believe, but also, first I should probably address 65 ter 935, 34 -- and 345. I think this is an attempt by the Prosecution to bring in the entire, for example, on 935, the IKM log, although, the witness didn't testify that she analysed the book in its entirety either the notebook, logbook or the IKM logbook, so just so that we have an understanding until that's verified because we will have witnesses who I think even the Prosecutor share with us a couple of weeks ago who will verify that they have made some additions such as the dates that we know about, that the Court not accept the evidence now but perhaps mark it for identification until we can see exactly who made those entries and why those alterations were made given her testimony today. Secondly, with respect to P02850, my description is rather vague and it just says that it's a selection of specimen and questioned documents samples used as Exhibit P724, and I'm just not able to see where P724 is but I think that it was the Blagojevic -- if it's the ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was in the Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's just not listed on the thing. It just has it as brief identification. If it's that, we don't have an objection to Mr. Jokic's ten page sampler going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You don't need to respond, in relation to P02850, but what's your position in relation to the submission of Mr. Ostojic regarding 935 and 345, 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour the Prosecution agrees it can be marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we agreed with that. Any further objections from any of the other Defence teams? So -- problems? No. Okay. So all the documents -- Mr. Ostojic, we are admitting without any reservation P02850 because this comes from Blagojevic and it was used extensively in the course of the -- both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. So all these documents are admitted except for 65 ter number 935 and 345 which for the time being will remain marked for identification. And they will remain so marked until the question as to the use that they can be made use them -- the use that they can be put to, is established, particularly with reference to other testimony that might be forthcoming. All right. Mr. Ostojic, do you wish to tender any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, but we may use some of the documents that we were provided with other witnesses so hopefully through that, we'll produce them to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon? Do you wish to tender any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that concludes the testimony of Kathryn Barr. And we can proceed with the next witness. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This witness, Mr. Milosevic, will need a caution, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our rules require to you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth. Please go ahead, read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Before we proceed with the examination-in-chief and the cross-examinations that are scheduled, that are planned, I've been asked to draw your attention to a particular provision that we have in our rules which spells out a right that you have as a witness and the limitations to this right. I'm referring to a witness's right not to be -- not to incriminate himself or herself. Basically what this means is that if in the course -- please look at me and pay attention to what I'm saying rather than looking at the accused, which you have already saluted on your way in. There may be questions put to you which you feel, if you feel that if answered could incriminate you, then you have a right to bring that to our attention and ask us to exempt you from answering such questions. This right is not an absolute one and because of that, we can decide to grant you such exemption or we can decide to compel you to give your answer. If we compel you to give such answers to so-called incriminatory questions, then you have a further right. Whatever you would state because you have been compelled to state it shall not be used as evidence against you in any subsequent proceedings that could be taken in your regard, except if we are talking of false testimony, which I am sure, I hope, will not be the case. So I just want to know for the time being whether you have understood what I am trying to explain to you in lay terms. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood you perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. McCloskey will go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Marko Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you were born?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 30 March 1964, in the village of Lupoglav in Kladanj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I grew up in the village of Lupoglav.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you do your regular JNA service?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did it in 1983 in Sarajevo. My service lasted 12 months and I completed it three months upon the completion of my university education. And I was supposed to do another three months but being a university graduate, I didn't have to do the three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you graduate in from university?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I completed the school of economy in Tuzla in 1979, and I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I gained a degree of engineer of protection at work and environmental protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia, what kind of job did you have?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia, I did not have a job. I was in Kladanj at -- waiting to be employed at the Bureau for Unemployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you become a member of the Zvornik Brigade when the war did break out?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the beginning of June or the end of May 1992. We fled to Zvornik municipality and there we joined the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say, "We", do you mean your family?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I meant just myself. My mother remained in the village, trapped there. One of my brothers was in Serbia and the other one was in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say "we," who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I meant just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you briefly outline for us your various positions once you began in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of May or the beginning of June, I can't remember exactly, I joined the army of Republika Srpska. We went to take up the positions in Tijanici and Brezik. That was at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your position in the beginning? What rank, what job?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I was just a foot soldier. I was in the trenches on the front line. I did not have any position or rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe to us how you eventually became the job that you had in 1995, which positions you went through?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the company that I served in within that battalion, we were relocated to the Setici stretch of the line. I was then reassigned to the command of the 1st Battalion, I think it was, and then for a brief period of time, I was the assistant commander for the morale of the battalion. After that, I also performed the duties of the assistant commander for security in the battalion. That was sometime in 1994, I believe. I don't know exactly up to when. I believe I stayed in that position up to September 1994 or thereabouts. After that, I was demobilised, and I was assigned to perform work duties in the Birac factory in Zvornik, and then again towards the end of March or beginning of April 1995, I was mobilised again and sent to the 6th Battalion as the assistant battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Were you -- and it may be a translation issue, but when you were sent to the 6th Battalion, were you the deputy commander of the 6th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. I was the deputy commander of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was your commander in 1995 in -- the battalion commander, that is?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ostoja Stanisic was the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you were the security officer for the -- a battalion in 1994, did you come in contact with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did have contacts. We would usually attend briefings together, when he summoned us to the brigade he would ask us to talk about the security of the line of the battalions, and intelligence data, should we have them about the movement of the enemy forces, and the way the situation looked around the -- around our defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the -- your professional relationship with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can say that he was very correct. Our dealings were at a very high professional level. Our relationship was very good and correct. And usually they boiled down to the military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And were you on duty at the 6th Battalion on July 14th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, I was in the battalion. I don't know whether I was on duty or not. I was not the duty operations officer on that day, but I'm sure that I was in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us when you first received information about visitors to the battalion area that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get a -- did you have communication with the duty officer of the brigade that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On a subject you have described for us before, I think in a March or excuse me a September -- March 14th, 2002, interview, and also in your testimony of 4 December 2003, in the Blagojevic trial. So can you tell us about that communication? What was -- what you learned?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the morning, between 10.00 and 12.00, the duty operations officer from the brigade called and I replied, since my commander Ostoja Stanisic was not there at the moment. He had taken a platoon of soldiers, some 20 of them or 30 of them to the brigade, because these soldiers were supposed to be sent to Snagovo, so I replied and the duty operations officer told me that in two hours' time or thereabouts, some imprisoned Muslims would be brought to the elementary school in Petkovci and that they would be accompanied by the security. He only informed me about all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that duty officer, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you receive that phone call?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the battalion command, the 6th Battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And whom, if anyone, did you inform of that information that you learned from the duty officer of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My commander, Ostoja Stanisic, returned after two hours. He came back to the battalion. And I informed him about that call.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you or your commander, Stanisic, do anything relating to that information?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just conveyed the information to my commander, Ostoja Stanisic. I don't know whether he did anything in his capacity as a commander. Since my commander was there, I was not duty-bound to pursue that -- the matter any further. When the commander was there, my duties were next to none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get any more information about those prisoners later on in the day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. As far as I remember, we did not get any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And later in the day, did you receive some instructions from your commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Sometime in the afternoon, he was also called from the brigade or at least that's what he told me, and then he asked me to look for Mr. Beara near the elementary school and to convey a message to him to report to the brigade command, and this is exactly what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know where Mr. Stanisic was when he received the information from the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you when Stanisic gave you the instructions to look for Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did you --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know who Mr. Beara was?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't. That was the first time I heard the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did your commander Stanisic reference Beara? Did he provide a rank or did he say "Mr.", if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember whether he mentioned any ranks. As far as I can remember, he only said Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so about what time did this happen, as you recall, that you got these instructions?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. In any case, it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do when you got those instructions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. When Stanisic gave him these instructions, where was he supposed to look for Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us more detail on when Stanisic gave you the instructions, where were you supposed to look for him?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: By the elementary school in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he give you anything in particular? Outside the school, at the school, some place else? Where were you -- what did he tell you about the location, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Commander Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing, just to go to the school, to find Beara and to convey the message to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I went to the school and since I did not know Beara, I had heard the name for the first time, at the crossroads of the roads leading to the school, I came across Drago Nikolic and since I had been his assistant, i.e. the security officer in his battalion, we had known each other, I asked him whether anybody by the name of Beara was there, and he pointed a person to me. I approached the man. We greeted each other. And I conveyed the message to him and the message was that he should contact the brigade and after that I returned to the battalion, and I briefed my commander, Ostoja Stanisic, as to what had happened. In other words, I was a courier on that occasion, and having done what I did, my mission was accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And where did you actually see and meet briefly with Mr. Beara and Mr. Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the crossroads of the main road leading Petkovci where the road forks off to the elementary school. That crossroads is some 70 to 80 metres away from the school itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And besides Drago Nikolic and Mr. Beara, who else was right there with them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The military police were there. I didn't know any of them. And as for the other officers, I did not see anybody else down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly how many military police officers were with Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not many, maybe four or five, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you notice any prisoners in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice any prisoners. I only noticed the security around the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you mean by that? Can you explain what security you noticed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I noticed troops in uniforms. Some were wearing camouflage uniforms and the others wore olive-drab uniforms, but I could not recognise anybody. I was standing rather far from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you having problems with the headphones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I'm okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any problems at any time, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, these few military police officers, how did you know they were military police officers, if you didn't know them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they wore camouflage uniforms and they had white belts, which was typical of the military police. The military police usually wore white belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could they have been from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. They were not from the Zvornik Brigades. I didn't know any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you -- was there a vehicle of any sort with Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Beara that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Down on the road, a few lorries and a few buses were parked. I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact number of those vehicles but there were buses and lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any people in them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about a car for Mr. Nikolic or Mr. Beara? Did you see any vehicle associated with them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there was a car for them, but there was a blue Golf III car there. I don't know whether one could associate that car with them or not but it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did Mr. Beara say anything to you when you reported to him what he needed to do?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't say a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you went back to the battalion command, did you go by yourself or did anyone come with you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I went there by myself, and I returned on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe you've said then you reported what you had done as instructed to your commander, Stanisic. And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I relayed to my commander, Ostoja Stanisic, in fact I informed him that I had relayed the message to Beara and then he in turn conveyed this information to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Beara or Nikolic come by your -- the battalion command post in Petkovci while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after you returned to the battalion command post in Petkovci that late afternoon evening, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is not completely clear to me. What do you mean what did I do? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you stay at the battalion command post? Did you go out into the field? Do you remember what you did after getting back there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on my return, I was in the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you stay there that evening?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you aware what was going on at the new school with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you do anything about those prisoners being there at that school? Did you go there to try to find out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't do anything because my commander was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you hear anything from the direction of the school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, yeah. On that day, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, that day, that evening, that night.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the late afternoon, there was gunfire coming from the direction of the school, isolated shots and bursts of gunfire, and there was also gunfire in our area in where our companies were. The whole of the afternoon there was shooting at the lines, but we also heard the gunfire coming from the direction of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you or your commander or anyone at the battalion do anything to look into what the gunfire at the school was all about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything. As I already said, my commander was there, and if anyone was supposed to do anything, that was the commander, and I don't recall him doing anything because we had other duties, other things to do, related to our defence area, the situation was very difficult, there was gunfire at the -- there was shooting at the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear large buses and trucks going back and forth to the new school and then towards the -- on the road towards Zvornik all night long the night of the 14th of July and the early morning hours of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything. We didn't hear that. It was too far for us to be able to hear anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do the morning of the 16th -- excuse me, the 15th, thank you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well in the morning of the 15th of July, early in the morning, my commander, Ostoja Stanisic sent me once again to the defence sector of the 4th Company in our battalion because we had received information that during the night, or in the late -- in the early evening, that two of the trenches had been abandoned or, rather, that they had been hit by a hand held launcher and the troops withdrew to the left and to the right of this trench and that left an empty space in our line. So on the orders of my commander, I went there with two or three soldiers to see what had happened and what needed to be done in order to re-establish the line so that we don't have those breaches in the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time in the morning did you go to the line to help fill this gap?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it may have been at 8.00 in the morning. As soon as I got up I went straight up to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Prior to you leaving at 8.00 in the morning, did you learn that many Muslims at that school had been killed and beaten at the school that night?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't learn anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Later, did you learn what had happened to the prisoners at the Petkovci school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, later on, when I was in the Zvornik hospital, because I was wounded on the 16th of July at Parlog, at our line there, and then some people came to visit the wounded soldiers and this is when I heard that those Muslims had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were wounded -- you were in the hospital -- sorry, about what date did you learn about that the Muslims at the school had been killed? Excuse me. Let me try that again. When did you learn, when did the people come to the hospital and tell you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it may have been -- I was wounded on the 16th, so it may have been after the 20th, after the 20th. Or maybe around the 20th. I can't give an exact date but while I was hospitalised and I spent maybe 10 days in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you provided your taped statement on 14 March 2002, did you tell the OTP investigators about meeting briefly with Drago Nikolic and Mr. Beara as you basically have testified today?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were first interviewed by the OTP, did you tell them that you had met Nikolic and Beara the crossroads, much like --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I said that was in Banja Luka. I think it was in March. I don't know the year. I think 2001 or 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, 14 March 2002. And also, when you testified on 4 December 2003, in the Blagojevic trial, did you say the same thing about meeting briefly with Drago Nikolic and Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I have various Defence teams wishing to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Ostojic, are you going first or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour or whatever you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose we can have the break now, after which you will have your cross-examination. It will be a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic. I'm going to ask you a number of questions here today in connection with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Introduce yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In connection with the material that you testified to. My name is John Ostojic and I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara. Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you discuss these events of July 14th 1995 with anyone prior to giving your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor on the 14th of March 2002?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically, sir, did you discuss these events on the 14th of July 1995 with an individual by the name of Radenko Basic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss them with Vlado Josic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss them with your commander, Ostoja Stanisic, at any time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. There may have been some conversations after that, but I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's try to be a little more precise. And what I'm asking you, sir, is prior to your interview in March of 2002. Did you discuss these events with any of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before March -- what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 2002 which was the date that we established was your first and only interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. Did you have any discussions -- did you have any discussions immediately prior to that interview with any of the individuals I mentioned; namely, Basic, Josic or Stanisic Ostoja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember all the conversations I had after having been discharged from hospital, after having been treated for my wounds. There might have been some conversations about all those events but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, just so that I'm clear and I often don't make myself clear, I know you were hospitalised from the 16th of July 1995 for approximately 10 days for injuries that you sustained to your legs. I'm talking about five years after that injury. Do you remember discussing these events with Ostoja Stanisic at all?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't remember. After that, I had to do work obligation. I had my own duties. I was a manager in two companies. That was my occupation. He was on another site. So we saw each other rarely, if at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- whether we discussed this matter or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are having some problems with hearing you. So if you could stay near the microphones and speak directly into them, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have as the dates of your prior testimony and the only testimony you had given in this Tribunal other than this one today in the Blagojevic case of the 4th of December 2003. I simply ask that you accept that date, although you may not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you remember, sir, if you spoke to Ostoja Stanisic about the fact that you would be testifying in the Blagojevic case on or about December of 2003?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I wouldn't say that I did. I don't remember having seen him around the time. Had I seen him, I might have told him but I don't remember having seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about after your testimony in December of 2003, to today's date, did you have an opportunity to speak with Ostoja Stanisic at all?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: About my testimony, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that we saw each other very rarely and if we happened to come across each other in town, this would be only a brief encounter and nothing else, and we never discussed this. I might have told him that I was in The Hague to testify, if I had seen him close to the date thereafter, but I can't remember whether I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When is the last time that you saw Mr. Ostoja Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The last time I saw Ostoja Stanisic was sometime before his departure, when he was supposed to testify here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Had you seen him after that, up until today's date?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I didn't. After his return from The Hague, I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How did you come about to see him immediately prior to his testifying here at The Hague? Who called whom?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that I saw Ostoja several times in town. I bumped into him. And on one such occasion he told me that he had been called to testify before the Tribunal and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
