utterances.text: You didn't discuss the facts, obviously, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you remember, and I know it happened approximately five or so years ago, your first interview with the Prosecutor in March of 2002, you said, I think, in your direct testimony that that was in Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you drove there or took the bus or how you got to the site where you were being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I came by my company car from the Novitet company. Ostoja Stanisic asked me to give him a lift. He had a daughter in Banja Luka and I had a relative there. I gave him a lift to Banja Luka and back. We went there together and came back together.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was about a two and a half hour drive there and back, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One way?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the way you can put it, two hours, two and a half hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about the facts of what occurred on July 14th, 1995, during that 2 and a half hour car ride to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what we talked about, but we certainly discussed other things, the everyday things. We didn't discuss any of the matters that you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Ostoja Stanisic ever learned from you whether or not you testified in the Blagojevic case on December 4th, 2003?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whether I learned?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we receive an invitation to The Hague to testify, you usually know that you have to go. At that time, the police was the institution that delivered.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- microphone we can hardly hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]-- went through Sarajevo, I don't know. But through Banja Luka I know that the police came to my home and delivered the invitation to go to Banja Luka and testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again, we have the same problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you can just -- because your voice is a little low and if you could just make sure to speak into the mike, sir, so the interpreters and translators could hear us that would help us a lot.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My question was slightly different, Mr. Milosevic. And that is, do you know if Ostoja Stanisic knew that you had testified in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If he knew? I can't confirm that he did. He is much better suited to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here today under oath, you don't recall ever telling him or informing him that you had testified in the Blagojevic case about the events of the 14th July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that I told him anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of Milan Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was he or what position did he hold in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time he was the assistant commander for logistics in the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what, if any, relation does he have with Ostoja Stanisic, this Milan Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know but I don't think there is any relations because he's in -- he's from Kladanj, and I really don't think that there is any relation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time have any discussions or meetings regarding the events of the 14th July 1995 with Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Dragan Obrenovic ever had any meetings with various battalion commanders in order to discuss the events after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have information from a -- although I'll have to be honest with you, as you usually am, from what I think is an unreliable source, which -- and for the Court's edification, the Prosecution's, I think it's page 11607, May 16th, 2007 transcript but I am purposely not identifying the individual to this person. You talked on your direct examination, sir, about spending the entire evening of the 14th of July -- on page 37, line 11 through 15 today, that you stayed at the battalion command that evening. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From this witness or source that we have, he states as follows and I just want to know if you dispute or agree with this on line 15 through 19. "The deputy" sir, that would be yourself, then he goes on to say, "The deputy and myself stayed there for a while at the battalion command and then we went back to the defence sector of our battalion. The right wing. The Sapna river area. And we toured the entire line to check out the situation, to verify what the status of the units was, the staffing levels and whether they had enough ammunition." Do you remember on the 14th of July 1995, sir, you went with another individual to the defence sector?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, we went to our defence sector, the 6th Battalion's defence sector quite often. I don't remember whether we actually visited this line, whether we toured it, then or not. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor asked you, you said that you were at the battalion command the entire evening, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the battalion command the entire evening. I know that there were many visits to the line on that day so somebody may have went there. I may have been up there for a brief while too, but I think, I believe that I was in the battalion command the entire evening, but if somebody saw me there at the line, that may be true, but it also may be misinformation, because on the 15th, in the morning, I spent the entire morning on the defence line in our defence sector, the defence sector of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if I could just turn to another topic so I could have the geography or appreciate a little better -- could you tell me the distance between the Zvornik Brigade command and the battalion command, sir? How far away is that in kilometres? And of course we are talking about 1995.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In kilometres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think maybe about ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how far was the Zvornik Brigade command forward command post from the 6th Battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The brigade forward command post was in the village of Kitovnica. I don't know the exact location because I never was up there at the forward command post, but because our forward command post of the 6th Battalion was also on the line in our defence sector, in Petrova Strana, and that was maybe three or four kilometres, I think it was not more than four, four and a half, five kilometres. That would be the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just remind us, if you will, where the 6th Battalion command was in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the old school in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Which is approximately 600 metres or 600 kilometres away from the new school in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's about 700 to 800 metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you testified today that you went to the new school in Petkovci on one occasion, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And at no time had you gone there more than on that one occasion, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how long you were at or near the school in Petkovci, the new school, on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe some ten minutes or it takes you about ten minutes to walk down there. Ten minutes to go there, ten minutes to come back, ten minutes to stay there so it was about half an hour all told to go to the school and back to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had this alleged encounter with Mr. Beara, correct, on the 14th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend with Mr. Beara conveying this supposed message to him?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A very short time, a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you testified on direct that he -- I'll get you the page number here -- that he said nothing to you, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything. I merely conveyed the message to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony in the Blagojevic trial, when you were asked to describe Mr. Beara, you identified him as being someone 60 years old with grey hair, correct? And that's --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's a fact, sir, isn't it, that that's all you remember about this supposed encounter with Mr. Beara on the 14th of July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a supposed encounter. It was an encounter, very brief, two or three minutes, and what I stated in my examination-in-chief, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you never heard him speak, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I had never seen that man before. I had never even heard about him. That was the first time that I saw him. And I never saw him again, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's true, sir, you don't know if this individual that you saw -- do you remember him having a rank on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether he had any rank on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you spoke a little bit on your direct examination about you leaving and coming to Zvornik. Is it true when according to your testimony in the prior case you state that you were expelled from your home town and then moved as basically a refugee in Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned your mother, that she stayed behind, I think you said, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not just my mother. There were maybe 50 people left in the village and they were all imprisoned later on and taken to the Stupari camp in Kladanj municipality where they remained until July 1993 when they were exchanged under the auspices of the International Red Cross. That was at Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And your mother was held prisoner in Stupari for approximately 15 months, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us who expelled you and your family, sir, and who held your mother prisoner for 15 months in Stupari?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were expelled by Muslims. That was in 2002 [as interpreted]. And my mother was captured by the Territorial Defence as it was styled at that time, of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They all put them together in one place, in the village, and took them to the Stupari camp in a truck and then they plundered and set fire to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, Mr. Ostojic because in the transcript page 51, line 16, this is supposed to have happened in 2002. I'm sure that is a mistake. It happened in 1992 or 1993 but certainly not in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to correct that. I know the answer too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in giving your answer, I don't know if it was just not heard or you may have misspoken with all due respect, when were you expelled by the Muslims as you state on page 51, line 16? It says in the transcript that that was in 2002. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in May 1992. 1992. In May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We didn't have it correct, and we don't want there to be a mistake in the record. Thank you for repeating that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One other thing, Mr. Ostojic, because I don't see in the record - it may have escaped me - but I don't recall having heard the name of this village where his mother and presumably himself used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I'll put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What village were you and your family expelled from?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I come from a village of Lupoglav in Kladanj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir I want to also talk about the events although not necessarily covered in detail of July 16th 1995, which is two days after the events of this alleged encounter with Mr. Beara. Am I correct, sir, that in the early morning hours of July 16th, you went with the 4th Company to assist them in the trench on the defence sector, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I went to the defence sector of the 4th Company. I didn't go there with the 4th Company but just with maybe two or three soldiers to check out the situation there where the company was deployed, because the line had been breached, two of the trenches had been abandoned, and this gap had to be closed so that if there were any combat later on, the next day, that we didn't have any problems there, because our troops were under threat if there were any gaps in our defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I am clear, why would you leave your 6th Battalion Defence line to go to the 4th Battalion defence line?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was not the 4th Battalion. It was our company, 4th Company, that was part of the 6th Battalion. The 4th Battalion was on our left wing. I think it was down there somewhere, Baljkovica or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. It was still your battalion, it was the 4th Company of your 6th Battalion, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that morning, sir, your 4th Company of the 6th Battalion sustained an attack in essence, correct, in addition to the attack that occurred the day before which you described in your direct where two trenches were actually hit with I think you said mortar fire, and they were abandoned. Now the next day, the same attack occurred, correct? And were you attacked? Yes? No?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, I went there on the orders of my commander with two or three soldiers to the positions of the 4th Company because we had been told the evening before that because of the mortar fire, the trenches had been hit by mortar fire, and that I had to check it out. Of course, if there were enough troops, we would have to deploy those troops in those trenches, if we were able to -- if we had been able to fix them actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now the 16th, in the early morning hours, there was another heavy attack, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was in the morning, at dawn, because I was to the left where the boundary was with the 4th Battalion, I was in the defence sector of the 4th Company, and then there was a mortar and artillery attack from the Muslim side, from Nezuk or maybe Medvedja, I don't know, but there was a lot of fire, and the trench where I was hit. There were a couple of soldiers there with me. The trench was hit, and then two Republika Srpska army soldiers were killed, one died on the spot and the other one died later on in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's Micic and Martinovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No -- yeah, Micic was killed. There were no signs of life. But Martinovic and I, under intense shell fire from the Muslims, we managed to carry him, although he was dead, on our backs to the nearest first aid point, and the other soldier, I think he was also from Tijanici he was in the 4th Company of our battalion, and he was hit in the abdomen, but he managed to get to the first aid station under his own power, but he died en route to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And although we know that you were injured on the 16th of July 1995, you were not injured on this early dawn attack, correct? You were in fact injured later in the day, about 2.30 or so, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Around 1400 hours, 1430. I really don't like to revisit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise for having to revisit that, I know that it's very painful, but during this second attack if you'll allow me to put this question, your company and battalion came under heavy fire again and you were injured among others and do you remember how many soldiers were killed approximately during this second attack on the 16th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the morning and throughout the day, we were under constant artillery fire from the -- by the enemy from Nezuk and other areas. There were shells coming in and also there was some fire coming from our rear because at that time, there were some well-armed Muslim elements, elements of the Muslim army, trying to break through from Srebrenica. So that we were -- we found ourselves in cross-fire and that was the situation at least until the time when I was wounded. That would be around 1400 hours. And I know that many people died. I know that because I was in hospital at that time. I think about 30 people, 35, 40 people, were killed that day. That's information that I have. That was at Parlog in combat with the Muslim forces and about 150 troops sustained minor or serious injuries. I'm talking about the Republika Srpska army troops. And then the wounded, including myself were hospitalised in Zvornik, in the Zvornik hospital. And the situation was very, very difficult. That was some intense combat up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I forgot to ask you this: How many people from your home town where you were expelled in 1992, how many of those people that you knew came to the Zvornik area after being expelled? Do you know the rough number?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact number. I know that there were many of them. I will tell you quite specifically for municipality of Kladanj and my village, Lupoglav which was part of that municipality that all those villages that were part of the municipality, so I'm talking about Serb villages with the Serb population. All those villages, people were expelled, they were all burnt down and they were all looted. According to my information, very few people went back to live where they have their old homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I appreciate that. Thank you. But my real question is were any of these former neighbours or friends of yours from your home town that were expelled, were they also members of the 6th Battalion in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Kladanj municipality is concerned, there were just very few of them, just some individuals. Milisav Martinovic, he was from my home area. We went to school together. But he was in the Zvornik Brigade but he was in the engineers. He was not in my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about Dragomir Topalovic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. Actually I know him. He was in the command of the 6th Battalion but he's not from my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, what I'd like to go back now is to the 14th July 1995 day and ultimately the purported meeting you had with Mr. Beara. Am I correct in understanding your testimony that you received a phone call from the Zvornik command Brigade and the reason you received this phone call is because your commander, Ostoja Stanisic, was taking 20 to 30 soldiers to the Zvornik Brigade, correct? Because they needed some assistance in the Snagovo or Crni Vrh area, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, when you -- when Ostoja Stanisic came back to the battalion command, where you were at, did he know already that the Zvornik Brigade had called you and told you that prisoners would be held in the new Petkovci school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he left the brigade to go to the line, to the defence zone of our battalion, and then he went back to the 6th Battalion command and that's where I conveyed to him that we had been informed from the brigade that some Muslims would come and that they would be put in the school. So I told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So at the time you told him that, based on just your answer now, you told him that they would be coming, they hadn't arrived yet, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had already arrived by that time or not. I simply told him that we had received notification about their arrival. But I don't know whether they had arrived by the time that he got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your battalion -- 6th Battalion command, did you have a duty officer on the 14th of July 1995 present?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think yes, there should be one, but I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you there should be one. During the course of 1995, specifically July, if you will, do you remember if that duty officer ever kept a logbook or a notebook to record any incoming or outgoing messages that he should have conveyed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who other than the duty officer of the 6th Battalion in the command is responsible to maintain a logbook or notebook of incoming and outgoing messages or orders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who that might be. Usually that would be the duty officer. If he gets a call, he makes a record of all the calls he received on a certain date. Now, I can't tell you whether this person really kept records meticulously or not. Maybe he just conveyed messages orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you, sir, as a deputy commander, don't you think it falls within your responsibility to make sure that those types of things are done by your subordinates on a regular and continuous basis?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the battalion commander should probably check whether this is done. It should be done. But I myself absolutely didn't do anything to control it. As I already told you, the commander told him that I should just make sure that the communications functioned within the battalion, that we were able to communicate with our companies, and the brigade. That was the only thing that I had to do, to make sure that it does. That's all I remember about my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know as limited as they were, sir, as deputy commander, isn't it true, though that if the commander Ostoja Stanisic was away, it was your responsibility to make sure that the subordinate soldiers would follow rules and procedures such as inputting in a logbook or notebook the messages they may have received, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really give you a very accurate answer to your question. The fact was that I was the deputy commander of this battalion, but you have to understand that I was just an ordinary soldier. I didn't have any rank. And I really didn't -- I had not encountered the rules of service or command manuals before, and I didn't read them at the time, to know exactly what my responsibilities and duties were. I was there to assist the commander whenever I felt that he needed it, and to be there in his absence, but I didn't read the rules so I really can't give you an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you remember, if you were present, whether Ostoja Stanisic called the Zvornik Brigade command to ask them about these prisoners at the new school in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him calling or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, whether Ostoja Stanisic at any time had a conversation with the Zvornik Brigade command regarding the events as you've described them of July 14th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I don't remember anything like that happening. He may have talked to them but not while I was there. I don't remember him doing that while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what I'm asking you. Do you remember ever being present when he did that, and you do not, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, I don't remember that he had any conversation with the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about the conversation where purportedly Mr. Ostoja Stanisic was asked to find Mr. Beara near or around the new school in Petkovci, near the crossroads? Were you present when Ostoja Stanisic purportedly received this phone call?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the battalion, when Stanisic received this call, he merely told him that I should go down there. Now, whether I was there that very minute, I don't know. I may have left the room or not. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I'm asking is for your recollection. Am I correct, sir that you don't remember that Ostoja Stanisic received this phone call from the Zvornik Brigade, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he received the call, he sent me there, on the basis of the fact that he had received a call. I don't know whether I was next to him or whether I was outside at that moment. He told me that he had received the call.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's all I want to clarify. Then you went purportedly to the Petkovci crossroads and you came back a half hour or so later, and can you just verify for me that you don't recall also, after telling, supposedly, Mr. Stanisic that you conveyed the message to Mr. Beara, you were not present when Mr. Stanisic called the Zvornik Brigade to inform them that the message was conveyed, in fact, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I conveyed the message to my commander, Ostoja Stanisic. He called the brigade. He conveyed that message in turn. And I was there. I heard him say that the message had been conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I have to clarify it, I apologise if I'm being somewhat repetitive. Are you telling me, sir, today, that you were actually present when Ostoja Stanisic called the Zvornik Brigade and told them that you had found Mr. Beara and the message was conveyed that Mr. Beara should contact the Zvornik Brigade command? You were there when Ostoja picked up the phone and made that call; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These are really very minute details. I conveyed the message to Ostoja that I had found Beara. That was my part of the job. And he was the one who was supposed to call the brigade and tell them that the message had been conveyed. And he actually did it. I don't know whether he told me that he had done that or whether I was there when he did that. In any case, I know that the brigade was informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor ever tell you that there is no record from the Zvornik Brigade command indicating that a "message was conveyed to Mr. Beara on the 14th of July 1995"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor ever tell you that there was no record in the Zvornik Brigade logbook or notebook or even the IKM notebook indicating that Ostoja Stanisic called them to supposedly tell them that a message was conveyed to Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They didn't tell me that during my interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As the 6th Battalion deputy commander, do you know why is it that neither in the 6th Battalion logbooks and duty books as well as in the Zvornik Brigade logbook and notebook and the IKM, there is no record whatsoever of there being any indication that there was this message supposedly conveyed by Ostoja Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer the question, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That assumes facts not in evidence. We have no record of any battalion logbooks, unless Mr. Ostojic has them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think the evidence of the witness and other 6th Battalion members and the protocol that's used established that they did maintain logbooks or else they wouldn't have a duty officer present for those purposes as he testified. So I don't have the logbooks. I was hoping that the Prosecution had those logbooks or maybe they can ask some of their witnesses if they hope to call in the next weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've been looking for battalion logbooks for many years. We don't have any. Don't expect to get any. But I'm always open for them if anyone wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless anyone else has any of these notebooks, the purpose of your question disappears.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to restate the question without including the battalion logbooks, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As a 6th Battalion deputy commander, sir, do you know why is it that in none of the logbooks from the Zvornik Brigade or notebooks or IKM books, there is any evidence to suggest that Ostoja Stanisic called the Zvornik Brigade and supposedly informed them that this message was conveyed to Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A very strange question. Whoever was on duty in the brigade, I'm sure that they did it, maybe they didn't. I can't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that you and Ostoja Stanisic - and you seem prepared for this which I'm glad you are - that you and Ostoja Stanisic made up this story about Mr. Beara because there was involvement of the 6th Battalion and members of that battalion in guarding the prisoners at the new school in Petkovci. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that what you're saying is absolutely incorrect, that you're being very cynical. This is making me a bit sick. Your question and what you are alleging, that we made this up is totally wrong, and I stand by my statement fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm not being cynical, sir. I'm trying to be as forthright with you as possible. I further suggest to you, sir --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was my impression when I heard your question. You -- you were accusing me, and this is a very grave accusation. I'm totally against it. I don't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Mr. Milosevic, you just answer questions. Otherwise, if you want to make comments, you address the Trial Chamber, and please do not engage into any direct exchange with any of the lawyers here. With lawyers, you just answer the questions that are put to you. You are not happy with anything, you address the Trial Chamber and we will address the matter. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I also suggest to you that you and Ostoja Stanisic concocted this story about Mr. Beara being at the crossroads near the new school in Petkovci during your trip or immediately prior to your interview in March of 2002 and that you spent two and a half hours with Mr. Stanisic in the car and specifically prior to when you received the subpoena for the interview, you met with Mr. Stanisic to get your stories straight. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're wrong, and I say that with full responsibility. You are not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I also suggest to you, sir, from other witnesses, such as Radenko Baskic [phoen] and Dragomir Topalovic, that in fact members of the 6th Battalion were indeed assisting in providing some security at the new school of the Muslims -- Muslim prisoners in July of 1995. You disagree with that as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm telling you is that the 6th Battalion, having suffered both on the 15th and 16th, attacks from the Muslims, that you and your commander, sir, sent troops from and soldiers from the 6th Battalion to the school in order to commit the crimes that the Prosecution has alleged has occurred. Would that be accurate as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We did not send anybody, and it is absolutely not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, send any members of your 6th Battalion, you or your commander, Ostoja Stanisic, did you send any of them after the events unfolded in July of 1995, to clean up the new school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not send anybody personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about your commander? He did, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The commander told me, when I was wounded in the hospital, that he had sent people to clean things up and that the villagers allegedly had asked for this to be done. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that Ostoja Stanisic sent soldiers from the 6th Battalion, with trucks, to do the cleanup; would that be correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Commander Ostoja told me that when I was in hospital, that he had sent them there. I wasn't there and I did not see that with my own two eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any former 6th Battalion soldier, sir, who was involved in the cleanup of the new school in Petkovci from July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I further suggest to you that because -- maybe I should strike that and start over. Slavisa Marjanovic was the commander of the 5th Company of the 6th Battalion, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My battalion had four companies, not five, and I believe that he was a member of the 2nd Company but I'm not sure. Slavisa Marjanovic, was it? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was the name. And I recognise you had four companies, but don't you remember, sir, that immediately prior to the fall of the enclave, Srebrenica, that a fifth company was created from your four companies of the 6th Battalion and Slavisa Marjanovic was placed as commander of this new company that went to Srebrenica prior to July 11th 1995? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One platoon from our battalion did go to the brigade in order to be sent to Srebrenica, and commander of that platoon was Slavisa Marjanovic. I don't know which company had been formed in the brigade, whether that was the 5th Company or some other. I really wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you learn, sir, prior to July 14th, 1995, that Slavisa Marjanovic was killed during the action at Srebrenica a few days earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We learned that the platoon that had been sent to Srebrenica as part of some company, with Slavisa Marjanovic, that Slavisa Marjanovic had got killed there and the troops that had returned from Srebrenica told us that. They were members of our battalion. Actually, they told us at that moment that he had gone missing. Subsequently it was found out that he had been found dead in the Srebrenica sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how many other soldiers from your battalion who went to Srebrenica were killed or died in July of 1995, during the action in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, only Slavisa Marjanovic got killed from our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I suggest to you further that you knew this information prior to July 14th 1995, as did your battalion commander, and given that your defence lines were being attacked on a regular basis, that the 6th Battalion, in light of the fact that there were these deaths or killings of Slavisa Marjanovic, the gentleman Micic that we mentioned, the other gentleman that it says, that results that you and your soldiers from the 6th Battalion went to the new school in Petkovci. Would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, sir, that no one from your battalion went to the school, as far as you know, on the 14th of July 1995, other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you share with us, sir, with whom, if anyone, other than Ostoja Stanisic, did you share this information that you met with Ljubisa Beara near -- I forget how many metres you said -- from the school area? With who else did you share that information?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just Ostoja Stanisic, my commander. If somebody had been present at the command from the ranks of the logistics, they might have heard that but the only person that I actually spoke directly to was Stanisic, my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me just develop or understand your time line. You get a call and I know it's rather broad, from 10 to 12 from the Zvornik Brigade that prisoners would be arriving at the new school and then Ostoja Stanisic is not there but he arrives approximately two or so hours later back to the battalion command, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already told you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you. I'm just laying the foundation. I appreciate that very much. How soon after Ostoja Stanisic's return did this second purported call from the Zvornik Brigade command arrive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe three hours or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that I'm clear, did you say three hours or 3.00?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 1500 hours, 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And immediately thereafter, it's your testimony that you went to the new school and that's where you saw a Mr. Beara for that two or three minutes, as you claim, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, sir, that you've had no contact whatsoever with Mr. Beara after that purported date, 14th July, 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If he has, that's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm suggesting to you, sir, that you and Ostoja Stanisic are fabricating this story about seeing Mr. Beara in July 14th, 1995, and that you started fabricating this story after Ostoja Stanisic met with Dragan Obrenovic to try to shift the responsibility of your battalion and Mr. Obrenovic to others. I'd be correct in that, wouldn't I, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that question already. You've put it to him more than once and he's categorically disagreed with you that this is all made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I -- I've added a function with Dragan Obrenovic, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he's told you already that what you are suggesting is not true, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, on the 14th of July 1995, whether Ostoja Stanisic also with you stayed the entire evening at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 14th? We were at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You and him together that whole evening, after 3.00 or so, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was at the battalion command and he was with me down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in the morning of the 15th were you asked to leave to go to the 4th Company to help with the attack that occurred on their trenches, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning of that day, which is the 15th, I went to the 4th Company. That was early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did Ostoja Stanisic accompany you to go to the 4th Company or did he stay behind with the battalion, 6th Battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I left for the 4th Company sector, the commander stayed back in the battalion. I went up there on my own, he stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about the 16th? Did he ever come to the defence lines or did he stay back?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th, in the evening, i.e. on the 16th around 1.00, both of us went to the line for the -- to the defence area at the forward command post. We spent the entire day there. While I was in the sector of the 4th Company, he was at the forward command post as the commander. I don't know who else was there with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. I have on -- next on my list, the Nikolic Defence team. Madam Nikolic, please go ahead and introduce yourself to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My name is Jelena Nikolic and I represent Mr. Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. I have a few questions for you that arise from your earlier testimony. First of all about the relationship that you had in the course of 1994 with Mr. Drago Nikolic. Earlier today you testified that you had been the assistant commander of the 6th Battalion and during 1993 and 1994 and that you were in charge of security?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that I was the assistant commander for security up to, I believe, September 2004 [as interpetered] when I was assigned to work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you mean 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1994. Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As you performed these duties, you had contacts with the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have contacts. I had contacts with Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I believe there is a mistake in the record. It says September of 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That is obviously a mistake. And it was corrected in lines 13 and 14. So in the meantime, Mr. Sarapa, as it is, I can't see you where you're sitting. First because of the column and secondly because Ms. Nikolic is also standing so if you could move a little bit further to your right, I would be able to see you better. Thank you. Go ahead, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The contacts that you had with the chief for security of the Zvornik Brigade, they were professional contacts, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You, as the assistant for security of the battalion, who did you receive orders from?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From my battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic, was he ever in a position to issue orders to either you or your commander?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will say that Drago Nikolic informed the commander if we were required to attend a meeting as assistants for security and then the commander would decide whether to send us there or not, whether to let us go or not. In other words, it was a matter of them agreeing on that rather than the matter of Drago Nikolic issuing orders to my commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To my learned friend's question you said that one of your duties was to maintain communications in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you what types of communications did you have between your battalion and the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We had three types of communication. One was the civilian land line, the other was the wire line, and the third one was the radio line, the radiophonic line.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you say wire line, does this mean an induction telephone line or a military telephone?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a military induction telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And if I understood your interviews and testimony well, then a military line is the one you most often used for your communication; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we used that line most often.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you only switched on the radio to control its functioning?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was done very rarely, only from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In communication with the companies, did you also use the induction military line most often, more often than anything else?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Because that line was the most secure line?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the most secure line and that's why we used it most often.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The companies also had a RUP 12 radio set, but you didn't use it for communication?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We did but only very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now I would kindly ask you to tell me something about the morning call on the 14th of July 1992, the call that you received in the command of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The date is 14th July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The call was about the arrival of prisoners at the new school in Petkovci. You received that call via telephone, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the secure line?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was the wire military line?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were told on that occasion that the prisoners would be brought to Petkovci, to the new school, within approximately two hours from that call?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the call took place sometime between 10.00 and 12.00 if I'm not mistaken on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, nobody asked you to inform any members of the battalion about that call or any of the company commanders or their assistants or deputies?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked you on that occasion to provide soldiers who might provide security for these prisoners because you were informed that the security would be on its way together with the prisoners on their way to the school in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Also nobody asked you to secure lorries or any other vehicles for these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked you to provide a firing squad to execute these people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever put any pressure on that -- to that effect during that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Also, nobody informed you about the destiny of these people, i.e. that they would be executed eventually?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the information that you received from the brigade command was just to inform the battalion commander that a certain number of people was on their way, accompanied by armed soldiers that belonged to other units, just by way of warning, not to engage your battalion in any way?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And this prisoner arrival took you by surprise in a way?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This event was not planned in any way previously. This was not something that you didn't know -- this is something that you didn't have any information before the 14th of July, before this call from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions regarding the event at the crossroads on the road in front of the new school in Petkovci, on the same day, the 14th of July, but in the afternoon. You received a message from your commander instructing you to go to a certain place to convey another message to an officer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you don't know whether at that time the commander had spoken to the duty officer or anyone else because you had not been present during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a duty officer or who it was, but I know that somebody from the command called.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you got there at the crossroads at the new school at around 1600 hours you said that you saw two or three military police officers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Or a few military officers who were not from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know the military police from Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not all of them, but I did know those who would come to our battalion or those that I worked with when I was the security assistant but that was a very narrow circle of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Madam Nikolic, we are getting back to the same problems with the interpreters. I think they are finding it difficult to catch up with you at the rate, at the speed you are conducting this cross-examination. So what I suggest is the following: Before -- between question and answer, you each allow a very short pause which would allow -- which would give time to the interpreters to translate to us into English and French, because I don't know if you know that that is happening. While you speak in Serbian, they are translating us -- translating to us in English, and if you overlap, they won't be able to translate everything. It's important for us to hear every single word that you are saying. Okay. Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me ask you this: Were there any troops from the 6th Battalion there in front of the school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time ask Drago Nikolic what was happening and what was actually going on in front of this school in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You merely went to the crossroads, you conveyed the message, and you went back?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would now like the witness to be shown Defence Exhibit 3D152. It's an aerial photograph of Petkovci, Mr. Milosevic, and what I would like to ask you is to have a look at it and for us to try to locate that spot at the crossroads where you had this brief encounter with the officers, as you testified earlier today. Mr. Milosevic, do you see in front of you on the screen this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be zoomed in as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is actually not very easy to discern things.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down a little bit? I think that's fine. Could we scroll down just a little bit and zoom in, if it's possible at all? A little bit further down. I do apologise, no, no, scroll up, please. I apologise. Just a little bit. Yeah, now it's fine. Now it's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you see this photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise on this aerial photograph Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This dark shadow, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The school.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So were you able to recognise it as the school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you now indicate to us where the road is, the main road, the road that you took?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, here it is. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the crossroads where you encountered Mr. Beara and Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Fine. Could you now please show us the road that would lead to the school and if you can do it with a broken line?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And if you could perhaps mark the plateau or rather the area in front of the school with an X?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to put the letters X, Y where this little circle is?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There, where the plateau in front of the school is?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, no, no. Actually at the crossroads where you put the small circle.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks] And the Y, yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you what is the distance between this area where you put the XY mark and the building, the school building itself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think maybe 70 to 80 metres. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And is the school on the high ground?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very small hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And from this road, and from this spot on the crossroads, could you see the plateau at the school?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, I would like to ask you if you could just put your name, your full name, and today's date here on this photograph, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just one more detail, Mr. Milosevic. Could you please mark the building where your command, the 6th Battalion command, was, in other words that's the old school building, if you can mark it on this photograph or perhaps we can scroll it up or down, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it needs to be scrolled.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, you can't see it here. Could we scroll the photograph down a little bit so that we see whether Mr. Milosevic can recognise this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can't be done now, Ms. Nikolic. We can save this, get the same photo, and then focus on the area that you are interested in, and we ask the witness to mark that one too. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance. I think that would be the right way to do it. So if we can then save this photograph now and then get the new one, unmarked, that would be 3D152, and then the witness would be able to mark the command and the old school in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you look at the screen, we see the same photograph. Now it's unmarked.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now, in fact I would like to ask for the photograph to be scrolled down. Fine. Do you now see on this photograph the old school building where the command of the 6th Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure. I know that it was on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if we were to scroll down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was down below the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think I should be able to mark it now. [Marks] Yes, yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you now draw a line, the route that you took as you went to that spot where you conveyed the message on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a little bit further down -- now it's not possible. But could we then save this photograph? I would like to ask to you put a date in the right-hand corner on the screen and your name.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in fact, it's the 26th today.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I forgot the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think that we have the same date on the previous photograph as the 25th, so it should also be corrected to stand, to show 26th of June 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic, and thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. We've got seven minutes to the break. Let me make a reassessment of the position. The Borovcanin team, are you going to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The Gvero Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The Popovic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to consult my client about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The Pandurevic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be very brief, but I would like to ask for a break before I start my cross-examination. I would like to take this opportunity to consult my client because that might cut short my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. By all means, both of you, both Mr. Zivanovic and you, Mr. Sarapa. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically that means that we'll give the opportunity to Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. Sarapa to consult with their respective clients and then we will resume in 25 minutes from now. And if we have no further questions for the witness, we adjourn -- we start with the next one. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, can I ask for a break of 30 minutes? Not 25. I'm supposed to meet with the next witness during this break and there seems to be a problem in to which room I'll be able to meet with the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. Absolutely no problem, Mr. Bourgon. It will be a 30 minute break then, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sarapa? Are you cross-examining this witness? Or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You go first? All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will not be asking you about those two days that my colleagues and my learned colleague from the Prosecution have asked you about. I will be asking you about some general issues. First of all, could you please tell me whether you were a duty officer in the battalion at any time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I, whether I was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Generally, in general terms, not only on those two days but did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall ever recall being a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as the assistant commander of the battalion, do you know what a duty officer does in the battalion, what his duties are?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the duty officer in the battalion received information from the brigade and from the companies, if they needed anything they talked to him and then he relayed all that to the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he received this information via communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, via communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you mostly used those induction telephones. Now I wanted to ask you whether the duty officer ever received any telegrams over the phone?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who in the battalion had the encryption documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about telegrams, do you mean encrypted telegrams or telegrams in general?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So when you said that the duty officer would sometimes receive telegrams, as far as you know, were you referring to encrypted telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know. Do you know who had the duty to decode the telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably the decoder, the person who knew how to decode those telegrams, who had the tables used to decode telegrams. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: Do you know where those telegrams that were received in such a form, encrypted and later decoded, who kept them? Where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As the deputy commander, you did not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, my name is Djordje Sarapa. I have just a few questions for you and then you will be finished. You spoke about the fighting that lasted well into the 16th and you mentioned some figures for the casualties, the dead and the wounded. Can we agree with the fact that the figures that you talk about are figures that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it true that you did not have any access to official numbers for the casualties?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So we could conclude that as regards the numbers of casualties, dead and the wounded, what you told us does not necessarily correspond with the truth, if it is contrary to what the official data say?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: When we are on the subject of the fighting on the 16th, it went on, but can we agree about the claim that the lines and trenches of the 6th Battalion did not move?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes. That they did not move on that date.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they moved at the time when I was there because we had to pull out to the reserve positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes. But how far was it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe about 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So we can say that this was a relatively insignificant movement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So we can say that you maintained the same positions throughout the day and that you successfully repelled the attacks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Sarapa in particular, and of course, Mr. Milosevic, allow a short pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it true that the members of the battalion command stayed inside the same room throughout the day, including the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The duty officer was in another room and we were all in an apartment near the old school, that was about ten metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And if there was a phone call for the battalion, could any of those present take the call in the room, those who were in the room?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually the commander took the call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And in the commander's absence, would it be quite understandable that you as the deputy would take the call?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I was there as his deputy, I would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your testimony ends here. We don't have any further questions for you, which means you're free to go back home. You'll receive all the assistance you require from our staff. Before you leave this courtroom, however, on behalf of everyone here, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony and also I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents? I imagine there are no documents from the Prosecution. From the Nikolic Defence team there are two and there are -- these are the two aerial images that the witness marked for us, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, according to the list that was submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, but could I just ask where they came from? The aerial images? Was that something that we gave you or is it -- the source, just so we have an idea of the time, the date of the pictures taken, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These are the materials that we received from the Prosecution. I believe that this is part of the collection that was prepared by Mr. Ruez, and I will be providing my colleagues from the Prosecution with the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So there is no objection, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I wouldn't imagine any objection from the other Defence teams so these two documents are so admitted. Can we proceed with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. I don't think we'll finish today. But I'm confident we'll finish tomorrow. Before you start your evidence, you're required by our rules to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Vanderpuye, you haven't indicated to the Court if it's the case of resorting to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no such application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So, Mr. Lazarevic, what's going to happen in simple terms is that Mr. Vanderpuye will ask you questions first and he will then be followed by the Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours, good afternoon, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lazarevic. I'm going to ask you to try to keep your voice up so that the interpreters can hear you and also to allow a short pause between the questions that I put to you and your answer so that everybody has time to catch up and the translations can go to everyone. If there is anything that I ask you that's not clear, just make that known to me and I'll do my best to try and rephrase it in a way that you can better understand the question. As a matter of first order, would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mitar Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 16th of July, 1957, in the village of Donji Sepak, Zvornik municipality, where I live today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What is your educational background, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have a vocational college, I'm a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you employed now?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am employed as a customs official in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
