utterances.text: How long have you been employed in this capacity?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I've been working in the customs service for the past nine years, in other words since 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you received any prior military training?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, I did my national service but that's it. And of course, there is my participation in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. When did you do your national service?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In 1979, it was in the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned your participation in the war. Did there come a time after you'd completed your --

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to what unit were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, they first made me part of some guards in the village until the mobilisation was called, and then I got the call-up papers from the military department and at that time I was in Kiseljak Battalion. I don't know the exact number of that battalion, the numerical designation of this battalion but it was in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did that battalion become part of the VRS formally at some point?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the battalion, as soon as it was formed, it was part of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did it -- was it subordinated to a particular brigade at some point?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, every battalion was subordinate to Zvornik Brigade in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, which was the Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did that occur with respect to the Kiseljak Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did the battalion that you were part of become part of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, naturally. According to the establishment, it was part of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you remember when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did your battalion eventually become known as the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the battalion Kiseljak split into two parts. One part went to Malesici and I went with it. That was the 2nd Battalion. As more people were mobilised, two battalions were set up and then at one point, this battalion where I was, which was headquartered in Malesici was the 2nd battalion. Now, I don't know whether it was the 2nd Battalion at the time when it was in Kiseljak. All I know is that at the time when I was at Malesici, it was the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe 1993 or late 1992. I really can't tell you but at any rate, it did split into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was your position within this battalion?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was a general services officer, or in other words, I was the assistant commander for general services.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that how you began your service within the battalion or did you move up to that position from another position?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, I was in a trench on the line, but most of the time I spent at this post, both in Kiseljak and later on in Malesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did you become assistant commander for general services?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1992, right at the beginning, maybe after a month or two, and after that initial period, I was at that post constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your position as assistant commander for general services, can you describe what your duties and responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I kept tabs on the strength of the battalion. I took -- I kept records about who was where on the line, on leave. I issued salaries and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises we didn't catch the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from issuing salaries and keeping records about who was on the line or on leave, what else did you do? The interpreters didn't catch the last part of your statement, of your reply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, usually, if somebody from the battalion needed to go out in the field, I would make a list, the commander would sign it, I would then take it to the brigade. So all the tasks that had to do with the drafting things, typing things, this was my job, and I did it on the commander's orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your keeping track of the whereabouts or attendance of members of the battalion, did you actually take attendance?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Not for the companies. I was in charge of the battalion. I couldn't go to the line every day to take attendance of the people who were on the line, whether they were there or not. It was the company commanders could did that. I just made a rota for the command, 5/2, five days we would be on the line and for two days we would be off. If the situation was normal. I never did rota for the companies. They were on the lines, themselves, and they would be on furlough and they were doing that among themselves. The companies did that. I was not in charge of that. I was not involved in that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was there a process by which the company commanders would furnish you with these records?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, not to me. They would provide that to the commander. They would provide me with lists if they went to the field, as for the attendance records, I didn't have that, I didn't know who of them was on the line, who was in the shift. I simply didn't know that and it was not up to me to know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were these records kept in a particular place?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, probably, for a certain time, and then it was destroyed because this was not an important document. This was not safe guarded for a long time. If something was of more importance, the archives were sent to the brigade. I don't think that this particular document was part of the archives that were kept, but I'm not sure when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities as far as concerns the keeping of records, then?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nothing particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the payroll records, did you keep those records?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As for the payrolls, they would get the money and everybody would sign, every company has a recording clerk, everybody signed and we returned the payroll lists to the brigade from which we actually got the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you keep the payroll list or a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The original would be signed and returned to the brigade from which we got the money. We never kept any copies, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your position as assistant commander for general affairs, to whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during your period in this battalion, how long did you remain in this position?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you from the beginning. Maybe not for the initial month or so, but after that, I was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 11 February 1996, I was sent to do work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the battalion command was centred in Malesici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately how far that is from Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: About 15 or 16 kilometres to 20. I'm not sure. Between a minimum of 15 and a maximum of 20 I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, during July 1995 were you a member of the command of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in 1995 July, can you tell us who the commander of that battalion was?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Srecko Acemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who was the deputy commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Stevo Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As best as you recall, who were the other members of the command during July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Stevo Savic was not there at that moment. He was at work obligation. Milorad Sarkotic security. He was also not there. He was in the field in Sarajevo. Vujo Lazarevic was in charge of morale. There were others. Vlado Acemovic; he was in charge of technical service; Zivad Pisic, the logistics; Zoran Jovic; and there were some couriers, I don't know what their names were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the infantry company commanders who were in place at that time? That is in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Stjepanovic, Miroslav Stankovic and Milan Radic. Those were the company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could, I'd just like to draw your attention to a different area, and I'd like to focus on your actions and movements in and around the time of the fall of Srebrenica and some period thereafter. First, do you remember when Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember when Srebrenica fell. I know it was in July but I am not sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is there anything that I could show you that might help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, if you have something to show me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Could I just have 65 ter 2469, please, in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could my colleague explain, Mr. President, before he goes and moves ahead with the showing of the document how he intends to refresh the memory of the witness? And whether the witness agrees that this will indeed refresh his memory? Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have gone through this before. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, I don't think it's necessary for me to establish how it will refresh the witness's recollection, how the witness's -- the operations of the witness's mind are the operations of his own mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I know how it's going to do that. My friend, my colleague, was killed on the 12th of July, and he was buried actually on the 12th of July. If that is what the counsel is referring to. Maybe that's what he's going to use to refresh my memory. If that is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, does that help you are remember around the time that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If that is what you had in mind, I know that on the 12th of July, my friend was killed in Srebrenica and he was buried on the 12th of July, if that is what you had in mind and this is what I stated during my interview with yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In and around this time, around the time that your friend had his funeral, and thereafter, did you become aware of anything unusual going on in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I learned it from commander Srecko Acimovic. Some prisoners had been brought in, but I don't know what date it was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you approximate or relate that to the date when your friend's funeral was?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think it was later than that but I'm not sure. I can't remember the date because at the time nobody kept any diaries. And it was 12 years ago. So it's very difficult for me to remember the details of when things happened. I think it was later but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you learned some information from your commander, Mr. Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tell us what you learned from him.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On that date, actually during that period of time, everybody was on the line because telegrams had arrived from the brigade. Before that, when the Operation Srebrenica was about to start, we had to be present on the line with 100 per cent strength. The commander went to -- home to take a bath. He was an exception. And that evening, he told us that in the school in Rocevic there were some prisoners that had been brought there earlier on. Should I proceed? Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you're asking me questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, maybe if I'll get you to slow down a little bit so that we can have this properly translated and give the interpreters time to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said that there was a requirement of 100 per cent strength. Could you just explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's the presence on the front line. Which means that everybody who was on the battalion list had to be there. Everybody had to be there save for those who were ill. Everybody else had to be on the line, all of us who had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The commander was an exception is what you said. Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The commander is a commander. He commanded all of us who were in the battalion. He went home on that day to take a bath. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you how he came to learn about prisoners in the school in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He said that he had arrived home and that his parents, his mother and father, had told him that there were some prisoners in the school in Rocevic and that he went up there to investigate what was going on. He just wanted to see what the matter was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall about when it was that he left to go home to take this bath or this shower?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he tell you what he observed when he went to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He saw some people who had accompanied the soldiers and he said that they were behaving in a very not normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he mention what people he saw, whether they were soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He said that they were soldiers but that he didn't know where they were from, who they were, and he even told me that he assumed that they were not members of the Zvornik Brigade. Whether they were or were not, I don't know, but he told me that he assumed that they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he made that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Because he didn't know them by sight. Commanders normally know his men. But he didn't know any of the security guards who had escorted those soldiers and who were guarding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he mention to you how many of these soldiers or security guards there were?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember him telling me. I don't think that there were many but I don't know how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he mention to you whether or not he went to the school alone or with somebody?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When he saw the prisoners, I believe that later on he talked to the priest and the president of the local commune in order to provide some food and water for those people who were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he mention how many people were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He said that the gym was full but he didn't know their number. How could he have known their number? He didn't count heads, did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he mention any other observations he made when he was at the school?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He said that the security guards were drunk, that they had killed a few people down there, and they had wounded a woman in that village, in Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he mention how he came into that information?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he himself saw that and told me about it. I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he describe any interactions that he had with other individuals that were at the school at the time, any conversations and things like that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I only know that he asked who the commander was and that he had problems with these people because they were drunk and they even threatened him, and that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think this would be a good time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop any minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Vanderpuye. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Lazarevic, between now and tomorrow, when you resume your testimony, you're not to communicate with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
